# Step 1: Scope

## Introduction

Write down what the ontology is for, and the questions it must answer.

The [scope](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-scope) is the part of the world your ontology covers. Without it, you can't tell when you're done. A coffee ontology could cover beans, roasting and farms forever. A [competency question](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-competency-question) is a question the finished ontology must be able to answer, like "Which drinks have no milk?" You can read the full guide to this step in [Methodology](../../../docs/METHOD.md#step-1-scope).

## What you'll make

A scope with a domain, a purpose, users and two things left out, plus six competency questions.

## Set the scope

Run the [`okb scope`](../../../docs/CLI.md#cmd-scope) command. The out-of-scope list matters as much as the rest:

```bash
okb scope --domain "Espresso-based coffee drinks and what goes in them" --purpose "Help baristas and customers compare drinks on a café menu" --users baristas,customers --maintainers "head barista" --out-of-scope "brewing equipment" --out-of-scope "coffee beans and roasting"
```

```text
Espresso drinks
  domain        Espresso-based coffee drinks and what goes in them
  purpose       Help baristas and customers compare drinks on a café menu
  users         baristas, customers
  maintainers   head barista
  out of scope  brewing equipment, coffee beans and roasting
  kind          application
```

## Add questions

Add each question the way a barista or customer would ask it. The last one asks about price, which you won't model. You'll see what okb says about that in step 8:

```bash
okb cq add "Which drinks have no milk?"
okb cq add "What's the difference between a cortado and a latte?"
okb cq add "What goes into a cappuccino?"
okb cq add "Which drinks are a variation of another drink?"
okb cq add "Which drinks on the menu come with chocolate?"
okb cq add "How much does each drink cost?"
```

```text
Added cq.1.

Added cq.2.

Added cq.3.

Added cq.4.

Added cq.5.

Added cq.6.
```

## Read the output

- okb numbers each question (`cq.1`, `cq.2` and so on). You'll use the numbers in step 8.
- The questions mix kinds (see [Why start with questions?](../../../docs/learn/competency-questions.md)): one filters ("no milk"), one compares, one lists ingredients. Good questions pull different parts out of the model.

## Check your work

Run the [`okb status`](../../../docs/CLI.md#cmd-status) command. Step 1 should have a tick. Then move on:

```bash
okb status
```

```text
Espresso drinks  · 0 classes · 0 slots · 0 instances · 6 questions

✓ 1. Determine the domain and scope ◀ you are here
     ✓ Domain and purpose are written down
     ✓ Users (and ideally maintainers) are named
     ✓ At least three competency questions
     ✓ At least one thing is explicitly out of scope
○ 2. Consider reusing existing ontologies
○ 3. Enumerate important terms
○ 4. Define the classes and the class hierarchy
○ 5. Define the properties of classes (slots)
○ 6. Define the facets of the slots
○ 7. Create instances
○ 8. Review against your questions, and iterate

Validator (steps 1–1): ✗ 0  ! 0  i 0   okb validate for details

Step 1 looks done. When you're happy with it: okb step next
```

```bash
okb step next
```

```text
Now on step 2. (To read a step's guide without moving: okb explain 2)

Step 2 of 8: Consider reusing existing ontologies

  Goal: Check whether someone has already modeled part of your domain, and decide whether to
  borrow, adapt, just reference it, or skip it.
  Why it matters: Reuse saves time and makes your ontology compatible with others. If you have
  to talk to systems that already use a vocabulary, reuse may not be optional.

Questions to answer
  • Is there an industry standard, taxonomy or controlled vocabulary for this domain?
  • Does any system you must integrate with already use a particular vocabulary?
  • Is there an internal list, spreadsheet, glossary or schema that already names these things?

You're done when
  ○ Reuse has been considered and recorded

Tips
  • Even a glossary page or an existing database schema counts as a source of terms.
  • Don't let this step stall you. 30 minutes of looking is usually enough for a first version.
  • Where to look: Linked Open Vocabularies (https://lov.linkeddata.es) searches hundreds of
  reusable vocabularies by term. schema.org (https://schema.org) covers everyday things: people,
  organizations, products, places, events and creative works.
  • W3C vocabularies cover common needs: SKOS for taxonomies and thesauri, Dublin Core for
  document metadata, PROV-O for provenance, ORG for organizations and OWL-Time for dates and
  times.
  • For design systems: WAI-ARIA roles (https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria/) are a standard taxonomy
  of UI components (button, checkbox, switch, tab...). The W3C Design Tokens format
  (https://www.designtokens.org) is the standard for tokens. DSDS, the Design System
  Documentation Spec (https://designsystemdocspec.org), is a draft schema for documenting
  components, tokens and themes.
  • You rarely need to import a whole vocabulary. Borrowing its terms and definitions is usually
  enough: okb reuse add --name ... --url ... --decision reference.

In the paper's wine example
  The paper notes a French-wine knowledge base or a wine retailer's list of wine properties
  could be imported, but chooses to build from scratch for teaching purposes.

Commands
  okb reuse add   okb reuse none
```

> **Common mistakes**
>
> - **Fewer than three questions.** okb asks for at least three.
> - **Questions that are really tasks.** "Build a menu" isn't a question the ontology can answer.
> - **No out-of-scope list.** Without it, every idea seems to belong.

## Next step

You wrote down what the ontology is for and six questions it must answer. Next, you'll check whether someone has already modeled coffee.
